questions.prompt: Which cost distinction between parallel and distributed DBMSs is emphasized?
options: A distributed DBMS cannot ignore long-distance communication delays and failures
A parallel DBMS needs no coordination because it never uses a network
A distributed DBMS may ignore message delays if it has a log
Parallel and distributed systems always make identical communication-cost assumptions
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes nearby, fast interconnects from remote networks with substantial costs and failure risks. Both kinds of systems can still use networks.

questions.prompt: What does data independence require when a query moves to a distributed system?
options: Return fewer tuples when data resides on remote nodes
Preserve the query's logical result when physical data locations change
Require users to name every node in their logical queries
Allow replicas or partitions to change join semantics
questions.explanation: Physical distribution should not change the logical answer. Optimizing network traffic does not justify silently dropping results.

questions.prompt: What atomicity requirement applies to a transaction accessing data on three nodes?
options: Each node may commit independently whenever convenient
Only the node holding the most tuples needs to commit
All parts must commit or abort according to one common decision
Committing on any two of the three nodes is always sufficient
questions.explanation: Atomic commit covers every participant. It is not a majority rule that permits part of the transaction to be ignored.

questions.prompt: Why is distributed failure handling harder than restarting one machine?
options: All nodes always restart together and need a fixed restart order
Local recovery can decide every transaction without consulting remote nodes
A delayed message proves that its participant has not committed
Other nodes may have continued and learned a decision unknown to the recovering node
questions.explanation: Recovery must agree with states and decisions that survive elsewhere. It cannot assume that every node stopped at the same time.

questions.prompt: What goals motivate deploying multiple nodes?
options: Better performance and availability, supported by appropriate mechanisms
Automatic atomic commit without a protocol
Eliminating concurrency control because data has multiple locations
Lower latency for every query regardless of network traffic
questions.explanation: More resources create opportunities, but do not automatically solve correctness or failure handling. Coordination remains necessary.

questions.prompt: What data-placement assumption is used at the start of lecture 22?
options: Every node stores every table in full
Data is partitioned but not replicated
No transaction ever writes
The system uses only one shared-memory machine
questions.explanation: The analysis starts with a shared-nothing system whose data is partitioned without replication. Replica-quorum rules should not be inserted into this model without justification.

questions.prompt: Where is the lock for a tuple stored entirely on node N normally managed?
options: Every lock table must be copied to all nodes so each can grant locks independently
Only the client manages locks, and servers always trust it
In node N's lock table
No lock is needed because the tuple has only one data copy
questions.explanation: Keeping locks near their data lets a node manage its own resources. A single data copy still requires concurrency control.

questions.prompt: What does the lecture suggest for a whole-table lock when the table spans multiple nodes?
options: Every node independently grants an X-lock on the entire table
Coarse-grained locks never require coordination
Grant the lock only at the node holding the query's first tuple and ignore the others
Assign a home node to manage the coarse-grained lock
questions.explanation: One authority for a coarse-grained object prevents contradictory grants. Independent table-level X-lock grants would not protect the entire table.

questions.prompt: N1 sees T1→T2, and N2 sees T2→T1. Both local graphs are acyclic. What is true globally?
options: Combining the edges reveals a deadlock cycle
There is definitely no deadlock because both local graphs are acyclic
Deadlock occurs only if both transactions originated at the same node
Remote edges do not count in a global waits-for graph
questions.explanation: A cycle can span nodes. Local acyclicity does not imply that the union of the graphs is acyclic.

questions.prompt: What simple distributed-deadlock detection method is presented?
options: Check only each local graph and discard remote edges
Periodically combine waits-for graphs at a designated node and search for cycles
Wait for participants to commit before searching for a waiting cycle
Examine only the youngest transaction's coordinator
questions.explanation: The global union exposes dependencies across nodes. Discarding remote edges would miss precisely the distributed deadlocks being sought.

questions.prompt: How do the main purposes of 2PC and 2PL differ?
options: 2PC controls lock acquisition, while 2PL provides atomic commit
2PC replaces isolation, so a scheduler is unnecessary
2PC coordinates atomic commit, while 2PL controls access schedules using locks
The two phases of 2PL automatically replace 2PC voting and recovery
questions.explanation: These protocols address different layers and can be combined. Sharing the phrase “two-phase” does not make them equivalent.

questions.prompt: What does the coordinator send in phase 1 of 2PC?
options: A final COMMIT before receiving participant votes
An ACK confirming that participants have already committed
A request to release locks before checking whether participants can commit
PREPARE, asking whether each participant can commit
questions.explanation: PREPARE opens the voting phase. A final decision follows only after the required voting and logging conditions are met.

questions.prompt: If 3/4 participants vote YES and one votes NO, what is the 2PC outcome?
options: ABORT
COMMIT because a majority agreed
Commit only the three YES participants
Treat the NO participant as an unnecessary replica
questions.explanation: Three YES votes establish readiness for only three transaction parts. The fourth NO may mean its required update violates a constraint. COMMIT would retain an incomplete transaction, so the outcome must be ABORT; 2PC uses unanimity, not majority approval.

questions.prompt: The coordinator times out before receiving one participant's vote. What may it do before deciding COMMIT?
options: Treat silence as YES
Abort the transaction
Commit only the participants that replied
Remove the missing participant from work already performed
questions.explanation: A missing vote does not prove readiness. Before receiving all YES votes, the coordinator may abort; a timeout is not an affirmative vote.

questions.prompt: After the coordinator durably records its decision, what happens in phase 2?
options: A majority revotes to reverse a recorded COMMIT if desired
Each participant independently chooses again using local state
The COMMIT or ABORT decision is distributed and ACKs are collected
Only PREPARE is recorded, and no decision is sent
questions.explanation: Phase 2 disseminates an existing decision. It is not a new vote that can overturn a durable COMMIT.

questions.prompt: Why must one participant's NO vote be sufficient to prevent COMMIT?
options: NO matters only when that participant holds most of the data
NO can be ignored if the coordinator itself is ready
NO prevents commit only if another participant also votes NO
The participant may have a constraint violation or be unable to complete its part
questions.explanation: Every part is required for the whole transaction, so failure in any part prevents a common commit. The NO voter need not have a special role.

questions.prompt: Does an ACK in phase 2 mean the same thing as YES in phase 1?
options: No; ACK confirms receipt or handling of the decision, while YES is a preparedness vote
Yes; both are votes sent before the coordinator decides
Yes; delayed messages can use the two interchangeably
No; YES means already committed, while ACK means only prepared
questions.explanation: Messages have distinct roles in the state machine. Treating ACK and YES as interchangeable would invalidate the decision conditions.

questions.prompt: Does a delayed message prove that its sender has crashed?
options: Yes; a timeout proves the node has stopped processing
No; a slow node and a crashed node may be indistinguishable so far
Yes; sequence numbers make delays impossible
The distinction is irrelevant because a slow node can always safely be treated as aborted
questions.explanation: Not receiving a message in time does not identify the cause. The protocol must tolerate delay rather than assume that the sender is certainly dead.

questions.prompt: If every participant has sent YES, may the client already conclude that COMMIT occurred?
options: Yes; each YES is itself the final COMMIT
Yes; no logging is needed
Not yet; a common durable coordinator decision is still required
No transaction can ever commit after YES
questions.explanation: YES means the participant is prepared to follow the outcome. Recording and distributing the final decision remain separate steps.

questions.prompt: Can 2PC alone replace concurrency control if the goal is to prevent dirty reads at one node?
options: Yes; PREPARE retroactively creates all required read/write locks
Yes; the final ACK repairs dirty reads already published
Yes; unanimous YES votes prove that every preceding schedule was serializable
No; atomic commit does not itself ensure a correct read/write schedule
questions.explanation: Two-phase commit and two-phase locking can work together, but are different mechanisms. Commit messages do not retroactively protect earlier accesses.

questions.prompt: What must a participant do before sending YES in logged 2PC?
options: Append PREPARE only in RAM, without flushing
Send YES first and write PREPARE after receiving COMMIT
Flush data pages and discard the transaction's recovery information
Persist PREPARE and the information needed to recover its prepared state
questions.explanation: YES is a promise that must survive a crash, so PREPARE must be durable first. A RAM-only record cannot preserve that promise after restart.

questions.prompt: Before which action must the coordinator persist its COMMIT decision?
options: Sending COMMIT to participants
Sending PREPARE to start voting, even before any votes exist
Any local update by a participant
Only after every participant has acknowledged COMMIT
questions.explanation: Sending COMMIT before persisting it could let a participant commit while a subsequent crash causes the coordinator to forget. Log-before-message ordering prevents this disagreement.

questions.prompt: Why must a participant's PREPARE record identify the coordinator?
options: So it can elect a replacement without learning the old decision
So recovery knows whom to ask for the decision
So an online coordinator automatically implies COMMIT
So PREPARE can replace the participant's COMMIT record
questions.explanation: A recovering prepared participant may need to query its coordinator. The ID locates the source of decision information; it does not replace the decision logic.

questions.prompt: Why does the coordinator's COMMIT record contain participant IDs?
options: To remove unacknowledged participants from the atomic transaction
To count a majority instead of requiring unanimity when votes are missing
To identify participants that may need the decision resent during recovery
To let participants decide independently without querying the coordinator
questions.explanation: The list supports completing dissemination and retries. It does not permit removing a participant's work from an atomic transaction.

questions.prompt: What does an asterisk next to a record in the 2PC diagram indicate?
options: The record may remain volatile and be lost in a crash
A message may be sent first, with flushing deferred indefinitely
The record's order is irrelevant if a transaction ID is present
Wait for the log to flush before sending the next message
questions.explanation: The notation marks a durability ordering requirement: flush before sending. It is essential for recovery rather than decorative.

questions.prompt: A participant recovers with PREPARE but no COMMIT or ABORT. What should it do?
options: Ask the coordinator for the decision, potentially waiting
Commit independently because it previously voted YES
Abort independently because that is always safe
Delete the transaction without undo or redo
questions.explanation: PREPARE records a promise, not an outcome. The same local log is consistent with a coordinator that has not decided and one that already committed elsewhere while its message was delayed. Ask for the permitted decision; timeout alone resolves neither possibility.

questions.prompt: A coordinator recovers with COMMIT but no END. What should it do according to the lecture?
options: Change the decision to ABORT because END is missing
Repeat phase 2 to distribute the decision and collect ACKs
Start a new vote and discard the old decision
Immediately delete all participant records
questions.explanation: A durable COMMIT fixes the decision. Missing END means completion work remains, not that the decision can be changed to ABORT.

questions.prompt: A coordinator recovers with both COMMIT and END. What further protocol work does the lecture's table require?
options: Always rerun all of phase 1
Replace COMMIT with PREPARE
No rerun of the completed protocol is needed
Undo every participant
questions.explanation: END records that the protocol finished, so the table specifies no further action. There is no reason to reopen voting.

questions.prompt: A participant recovers with PREPARE and COMMIT, but its ACK may have been lost. What is appropriate?
options: Abort because no durable local ACK record is visible
Discard COMMIT and return to voting
Wait for every other local transaction to commit before deciding
Send an ACK to the coordinator
questions.explanation: The local decision is already known to be COMMIT, so the participant completes acknowledgement. A lost ACK does not change the outcome.

questions.prompt: A participant has not logged PREPARE when it discovers that the coordinator is unreachable. What may it do?
options: Abort locally
It must commit independently
It must retain locks forever in every case
Treat the coordinator's silence as a YES vote
questions.explanation: Before entering the prepared state, the participant has not promised to await the final decision and may abort. The rules change after PREPARE.

questions.prompt: What do message numbers 1,2,3,... for each sender/receiver/transaction combination help with?
options: Guaranteeing zero network delay
Detecting missing or out-of-order messages
Replacing WAL automatically
Removing the need for transaction IDs
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers let the receiver detect gaps. They neither prevent delays nor make data durable.

questions.prompt: A receiver gets message 5 after receiving only 1,2,3. What should it do under the lecture's mechanism?
options: Process 5 immediately and discard 4 if it later arrives
Treat the higher sequence number as proof of COMMIT
Buffer 5 until 4 arrives, then process messages in order
Tell the sender to omit message 4 so the gap disappears
questions.explanation: The receiver retains message k+1 until it has received 1..k. A larger sequence number does not supply missing prerequisite state.

questions.prompt: Why does a participant retain locks while awaiting the 2PC decision under strict 2PL?
options: To make PREPARE identical to a final COMMIT
To remove the coordinator's need to persist its decision
To let all other transactions read temporary data without S-locks
To prevent others from observing or overwriting unfinished transaction state
questions.explanation: Retaining locks preserves isolation through the prepared phase. It may reduce concurrency rather than improve speed.

questions.prompt: How must COMMIT processing coordinate log flushing and lock release?
options: Use an appropriate atomic completion boundary and ordering so visibility does not precede durable state
Release locks before COMMIT is durable and flush whenever convenient afterward
Skip COMMIT flushing if an X-lock was held
Persist only PREPARE and release locks without learning the final decision
questions.explanation: Other transactions must not see a state whose outcome lacks durable protection. Locks do not replace logging.

questions.prompt: Does “abort locally” under strict 2PL let a prepared participant override the 2PC decision at will?
options: Yes; any PREPARE can be discarded after a timeout
No; local processing must still respect the 2PC state and decision
Yes; strict 2PL makes COMMIT unnecessary
No; no transaction may ever abort
questions.explanation: Local undo without cascading readers is an isolation benefit, not authority to override the shared commit decision. After durable PREPARE, another participant may already have committed. Resolve the 2PC outcome first, then carry out the permitted local completion and release.

questions.prompt: What can happen when the coordinator is unreachable after a participant has prepared?
options: Every participant can safely commit after a timeout
Every prepared participant can independently abort without asking
The participant can block while retaining locks
It can release locks and decide later while still following strict 2PL
questions.explanation: A prepared participant without a decision may have to wait, and its locks can delay other transactions. It cannot commit independently merely to improve availability.

questions.prompt: Why does adding machines not automatically make 2PC more available?
options: A new node automatically replaces the coordinator without agreement on state
Extra partitioning makes every transaction local
More participants allow majority YES votes to replace unanimity
More components and coordination create additional failure opportunities that can impede progress
questions.explanation: Scale-out adds resources but also failure points and coordination. It does not automatically remove blocking on the coordinator.

questions.prompt: How do safety and availability differ in the blocking-2PC example?
options: Preserving one consistent decision can require waiting and reduce service availability
Waiting always proves that atomic-commit safety has failed
Availability means every transaction must commit
Safety permits one participant to abort while another commits after a timeout
questions.explanation: A protocol can remain safe while failing to make progress without decision information. Availability does not mean committing every request.

questions.prompt: Prepared T1 holds a lock for a long time. T2 is unrelated to its coordinator but needs the same object. What can happen?
options: T2 always bypasses the lock because it is on another node
T2 can also be blocked by T1's lock
T2 treats T1's PREPARE as COMMIT and reads the object
T2 aborts T1 locally without knowing the global decision
questions.explanation: Blocking propagates through locked resources. T2 cannot bypass concurrency control simply because it is not part of T1.

questions.prompt: How is Paxos Commit mentioned in the lecture?
options: As an exact synonym for basic 2PC
As a rule allowing a majority of business participants to commit while discarding the rest
As a further approach to availability beyond the lecture's detailed treatment
As a way to omit logging while recovering forgotten decisions
questions.explanation: The lecture presents it as an extension, not as a quorum rule for discarding required transaction parts. Consensus by a majority does not replace the requirement that every participant be ready to commit.
